title: Berkshire 2007 letter: great, good and gruesome businesses, See's Candy economics, and Buffett's mistakes
summary: Buffett explains what makes a great business (an enduring moat, low capital needs, not dependent on a superstar manager), contrasting See's Candy, FlightSafety and airlines. He owns up to unforced errors (Dexter, a TV station, US Air), shows why active management must trail index funds, and criticizes corporate accounting games.

principles.text: Seek businesses with an enduring moat protecting high returns on capital; a moat that must be rebuilt constantly is no moat.
principles.quote: A truly great business must have an enduring “moat” that protects excellent returns on invested capital.

principles.text: A business that needs a superstar manager to produce great results is not itself a great business.
principles.quote: But if a business requires a superstar to produce great results, the business itself cannot be deemed great.

principles.text: The worst business grows fast, needs heavy capital, and earns little; the best grows earnings with almost no new capital.
principles.quote: The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money.

principles.text: Redeploy a great business's surplus cash into other businesses rather than reinvesting where it was earned.
principles.quote: There’s no rule that you have to invest money where you’ve earned it.

principles.text: Active investors as a class must trail passive ones because of costs; beware advisers promising double-digit equity returns.
principles.quote: That means that the passive group – the “know-nothings” – must win.

principles.text: Prefer a partial stake in a great business over owning all of a mediocre one.
principles.quote: It’s better to have a part interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.
